newsitem.title: PERU: Peru crisis raid seen strengthening military's hand.
newsitem.headline: Peru crisis raid seen strengthening military's hand.

text.p: The Peruvian military's dramatic rescue of hostages at the Japanese ambassador's home boosted the image of a much-criticised institution and strengthened its already strong grip on power, analysts said.

Rocked by accusations of murder and torture, and often accused of holding excessive sway over President Alberto Fujimori, the armed forces regained lost pride with the internationally acclaimed raid that saved 71 hostages.

"This operation restores the legitimacy of the military institutions in the eyes of the people," David Scott Palmer, a leading author on Peruvian guerrillas, told Reuters by telephone from Boston. He said the military probably would get funds for new equipment and refurbishing as a result of the decisive strike that ended the 126-day standoff.
But there was also concern the army's influence over Fujimori could grow.
Only Fujimori, a select group of generals and advisers and the 140 troops involved knew in advance of Tuesday's assault, which was even kept secret from Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto.
"Certainly the military has demonstrated its relationship with Fujimori," Scott Palmer added.

Many Peruvians think their leader is too close to hawkish military leaders, particularly the head of the armed forces, Gen. Nicolas de Bari Hermoza Rios, and intelligence service adviser Vladimiro Montesinos. Although he is believed to be Fujimori's most trusted aide, Montesinos is rarely seen in public and never makes public statements.

"Their relative power vis-a-vis Fujimori at least has been manifested the way it was never manifested before," Hernando de Soto, director of Lima's Institute of Liberty and Democracy, said. "You have a personal agenda of Montesinos and Hermoza which we know very little about, and which people complain about," de Soto said.
In a deliberate public appearance, the two men toured the burned-out siege site together on Wednesday to survey the scene of their successful operation.

Fujimori's close ties to the military stem from his so-called self-coup in April 1992, when the armed forces backed his strategy to dissolve Congress and the judiciary and rewrite the constitution to strengthen his grip on power.

"This is the second time, counting the self-coup in 1992, that the military methodology brings success (to Fujimori) and I am worried that he is using this to consolidate power and that the military are using this once again to gain impunity," Carlos Ivan Degregori, an expert on guerrilla warfare, said.

Former Congressman Manuel Noreyra said recent accusations in the local media that one intelligence service agent was murdered and another tortured by the military for leaking information had pushed the armed forces to storm the residence to stop an avalanche of criticism. "They were threatened and now they have a large curtain (to hide behind)," Noreyra said.
But government supporters denied the military's role would be strengthened as a result of the successful conclusion to Latin America's longest hostage siege.

"The army has always been strong in this government, I don't think this will change in the immediate term," said Congressman Carlos Ferrero Costa of Fujimori's Change 90-New Majority party, who himself has called several times for a distancing between the military and the government.

Peruvian writer Mario Vargas Llosa, who unsuccessfully challenged Fujimori in the 1990 presidential race, said in Argentina that Fujimori would use the hostage crisis triumph to gloss over human rights violations in his government.

"The authoritarian regime of Mr. Fujimori was in a very complicated situation because of the appearance of dismembered (people) and tortures," Vargas Llosa added, referring to the case of the intelligence officers.

And despite the success of the military raid on the residence, the armed forces now face new accusations of excesses carried out during the assault. One hostage, two army officers and all 14 Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels were killed in the attack.

Military sources told Reuters on Thursday that two of the guerrillas had been executed after being captured and others were killed as they tried to surrender. Two men were captured, told to stand against a wall and shot with separate bursts of gunfire one after the other, the sources said.
At least one teenage girl rebel was also shot to death despite yelling to try to give herself up, according to an intelligence agent who monitored the raid through listening devices.
